newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin gives some details on Yeltsin op, no date.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin gives some details on Yeltsin op, no date.

text.p: The Kremlin drip-fed the media with information about President Boris Yeltsin's heart operation on Monday as doctors got ready to set a date.

A Kremlin spokesman said Russian specialist Renat Akchurin would lead the operation team at the Cardiology Research Centre, a jumble of glass and concrete buildings in a western Moscow suburb. But he could not say when it would start.
Security was tight outside the building on Monday. Police sniffer dogs checked cars and guards patrolled the grounds.
The Kremlin press office said it would release a bulletin on Yeltsin's health and Interfax news agency quoted medical sources as saying a doctors' meeting would start at 4 p.m. (1300 GMT).

The doctors, including pioneering U.S. surgeon Michael DeBakey, were due to decide if Yeltsin, 65, was fit enough for the triple or quadruple bypass -- which will improve the blood supply to his heart.
DeBakey arrived in Moscow from the United States on Sunday but Russian officials whisked him away from the airport without letting him talk to a crowd of waiting journalists.
DeBakey, 88, will be a consultant during the operation, but will not wield the surgeon's knife. He said last week he expected doctors to operate early this week.

Yeltsin, breaking with a long Kremlin tradition of secrecy about the health of its leaders, said on September 5 he would have an operation on his heart and doctors said later that month that it would take 6-10 weeks to prepare him for surgery.
The six-week deadline expires this week. Doctors have treated the Russian president for blood and thyroid problems and he looked healthy in recent television appearances.

Yeltsin has already handed some powers over to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who will deputise during the operation and who was chairing a meeting of the influential Security Council in Moscow on Monday.
The council, normally chaired by the president, groups senior Russian ministers and security officials.
The Kremlin has made clear Yeltsin will give Chernomyrdin control of Russia's nuclear arsenal just before the surgery. A second decree hours later will annul this, if all goes according to plan.

Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and concern about his health has overshadowed the political and economic scene since he defeated Communist Party candidate Gennady Zyuganov on July 3 to win a second term in the Kremlin.

Zyuganov's communists have kept a low profile in the State Duma lower house of parliament, where they are the largest single party. But their candidates have done well in many of the local elections being held across Russia.
The local polls, being held over a six-month period ending in February, allow voters to choose a new regional governor.
But the polls are important on a national level as well because the regional governors also become members of the Federation Council upper house of parliament.
A communist-backed candidate won a seat in the upper house on Sunday and will represent the remote northeastern region of Magadan, location of many of Soviet-era dictator Josef Stalin's prison camps.
A second vote was won by the candidate representing Vladimir Zhirinovsky's extreme nationalist Liberal Democratic Party.

Zhirinovsky, a flamboyant and at times outrageous character, had campaigned actively for Yevgeny Mikhailov in the northwestern region of Pskov, which borders the Baltic former Soviet republic of Estonia.

Russia has an unresolved border dispute with Estonia in the Pskov region and the Kremlin's relations with the Baltic state, complicated by the presence of a large ethnic Russian minority there, have been troubled.
